newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-MCLAREN BOSS SLAMS RULE CHANGES.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-MCLAREN BOSS SLAMS RULE CHANGES.

text.p: McLaren team chief Ron Dennis on Tuesday hit out at Formula One's latest rule changes when he unveiled the Mercedes Benz-powered car he hopes will make his team winners again this year for the first time since 1993.

Dennis, managing director of the McLaren team, said he was very unhappy at new regulations which limit testing for the teams and criticised the latest situation relating to the new Concorde Agreement between the teams and the ruling body FIA (International Motoring Federation).

Speaking at McLaren's headquarters, Dennis said: "I don't think any team can get the amount of testing it wants to now. I can understand the philosophy behind the changes, but I am a little free-market orientated and testing, although expensive, is the cheapest way of developing a racing car."
Dennis warned that instead of costs being cut by the restrictive testing rules, they may increase because of them.
He said: "Teams may be forced to simulate improvements because if you can't evaluate them in the real environment then you will have to do it on a computer."
Talking about the Concorde Agreement, introduced late last year, Dennis admitted he was still unhappy at the terms which the majority of teams had accepted in signing it.
McLaren, Williams and Tyrrell refused to sign the agreement and will not receive any of the financial benefits, such as a travel budget, which will be paid to the other teams which have signed it.

Dennis said he could not see a happy outcome for the problem, but explained: "It is an extremely difficult situation and there is no simple answer. It is not fully understood by most people, but I hope in the course of the next few days to positively solve the situation and find the most sensible way forward."

The new Mercedes-powered McLaren MP4/12, painted in a striking orange colour scheme for its initial testing period before its official launch on February 14, looked very similar in design to its predecessor.
But Dennis said 90 per cent of the car was entirely new.
Many of the changes were enforced by the new latest technical regulations. These include a rear impact zone, a collapsible steering column and reduced winglet area.
From the outside, the most obvious new features are a lower raised front nose and a much lower seating position for the driver.
"We have gone through a long process to get the driver low down and where he can function properly," explained Dennis.

Briton David Coulthard, who will partner Finland's Mika Hakkinen as the team's driving team, said he would reserve judgment on the new position until after testing which begins at Jerez in Spain on Wednesday.
"It will be more physical to drive than before, but just how much I don't know yet," said Coulthard. "But if it is quick, it won't really matter. The detail looks right and the finish looks good."
Dennis added on his hopes for 1997: "I very much want to win, although not winning will not be a problem to me.

"There are some things you can quantify and some things you can't, such as the car balance, but I would be surprised if we haven't improved in areas where we can. It will be a question of just how much we have improved and how little our opponents haven't."
